question.text:
You are analyzing the performance of two equity funds over the past five years. Here are the annual returns: Fund X: 8%, 12%, -5%, 15%, 10% Fund Y: 10%, 9%, -3%, 18%, 8%
Rank the funds based on cumulative return over the five-year period.

answer.text: Fund Y is higher than Fund X
Fund X is higher than Fund Y
Both funds have the same cumulative return
Cannot determine from the given data

explanation.text: The Logic: Cumulative return is the compounded product of (1 + annual return), not the sum. Fund X: (1.08)(1.12)(0.95)(1.15)(1.10) - 1 = 45.76%. Fund Y: (1.10)(1.09)(0.97)(1.18)(1.08) - 1 = 49.86%. Fund Y wins because its positive years compound off a smaller negative-year drag (-3% vs -5%). The Trap: The tempting shortcut is to simply add the annual returns: Fund X sums to 40% and Fund Y to 42%, making Fund Y look marginally better by 2 percentage points. That arithmetic ignores compounding and understates both numbers; the 'same answer' trap (option C) and the 'cannot determine' escape (option D) both assume the data is insufficient, but the returns are fully specified. Cross-Exam Context: Cumulative/point-to-point return mechanics appear in NISM-XV (Research Analyst), NISM-XXI-B (PMS Managers), and NISM-XIX-C (AIF Managers) whenever past-performance math is tested. Distributor's Pro-Tip: When a client asks 'which fund did better over 5 years?' always quote cumulative (point-to-point) return or CAGR, never the arithmetic average of annual returns; a single deep drawdown year can flip the ranking and clients respect you for showing the compounded reality.
